projects.title: Lanterns of Selvane
projects.tagline: A small-party action-exploration RPG in the browser, on a procedurally generated garden world.
projects.body:
Up to four players explore a seeded world with a 6 km radius, laid out in rings of biomes. Landmarks
are placed so the next one is always visible on the horizon, and shelter comes from lore-rich shrines,
the Lanterns, that you kindle rather than build. The pitch is *Phantasy Star Online × Breath of the
Wild × Valheim × Tunic*.

It's TypeScript end to end: three.js in the browser, and a Node world server over WebSockets with
SQLite. World generation is a pure, deterministic package that client and server share. Parties,
companions, enemy tiers, radar, LODs and an asset viewer are all in. Since November an autonomous
Claude Code loop works the backlog overnight. It playtests its own changes and opens pull requests for review in the morning.

images.caption: Midday in the meadow ring, with floating islands on the horizon
The Heartwell's beam at the centre of the world
A whole generated world (seed 1), biome rings from the centre out

projects.title: Creature pipeline
projects.tagline: Local text-to-concept-art-to-3D for the game's creatures, entirely on the workstation's GPUs.
projects.body:
A batch pipeline that writes concept sheets for each creature with an open image model, cuts out the
subject with BiRefNet, and lifts the best views into textured 3D meshes with TRELLIS. Each species
gets several style passes (classic, fern, faceted, woolly…) to choose from before modelling.

images.caption: Concept pass for a cinder hound

projects.title: Woodshed
projects.tagline: A Rocksmith-style piano trainer that runs in the browser over Web MIDI.
projects.body:
Plug in a MIDI keyboard and jam with a backing band in the Jam Room (band styles, missions, a coach,
key walks, free play with a chord trail and .mid export), or work through 8 arcade games and 45
lessons in 10 units, with a circle-of-fifths view. An "anti-laurels" layer keeps a quick-eared
player from coasting: a key heatmap, a Laurels Meter and a Daily Woodshed.

There's no build step and no server state. It's plain scripts on one namespace, and progress lives
in the browser.

images.caption: The Jam Room: a progression, the next chord, a coach and a mission
Eight arcade games, each drilling one jam skill
The circle of fifths, with every chord in the key

projects.title: Pianoforge
projects.tagline: Turned a solo piano recording into a playable 88-key sampled instrument.
projects.body:
Drop in a recording and it separated the piano from everything else (Demucs), transcribed the notes
(Transkun), analysed each note's partials, calibrated an additive-plus-noise model against the
recording by analysis-by-synthesis, and exported an SFZ instrument. Retired in November 2026.

projects.title: Narrated story video
projects.tagline: A short narrated video built from a JSON scene script and local text-to-speech.
projects.body:
Each scene in a JSON script lists its lines. Kokoro voices every line separately and trims its silence,
and the build lays out the film's whole timeline, so captions and animation cues land exactly on the
words. To change the video, you edit the script and rebuild.

projects.title: FT-891 Shack Console
projects.tagline: A browser console for a Yaesu FT-891 HF radio, with CAT control, a waterfall, and FT8 and CW decoding.
projects.body:
It talks to the radio through a DigiRig Mobile interface. A beginner-friendly Simple view sits beside a
Pro view with every CAT control, meters and a live waterfall. It decodes FT8 with WSJT-X's jt9, and
decodes Morse with automatic pitch and speed, giving each transmitter its own line.

It knows which frequencies each US licence class may use (47 CFR §97.301/305/307), estimates RF
exposure from FCC OET 65 duty factors, and shows band conditions from NOAA and ionosonde data. It's
receive-only by default, and a Bluetooth knob can tune the VFO.

images.caption: The Pro view, with every CAT control, meters and the waterfall (radio off, placeholder callsign)
The Simple view for new operators (radio off, placeholder callsign)

projects.title: CW decoder for SDR++
projects.tagline: An SDR++ module that copies Morse automatically, both the station you're tuned to and every other keyed signal nearby.
projects.body:
It's a C++ port of the shack console's decoder: automatic pitch and speed, a false-lock guard, and a
phase-slope trick that starts a new line for each transmitter, each at its own speed. Decoded text is
split into words and annotated (Q-codes, prosigns, signal reports, grid squares with distance,
POTA/SOTA references, callsign prefixes), with optional callbook lookups. Nothing like it existed for
SDR++ on Linux.

images.caption: Decoding a 40 m CW signal, with every nearby transmitter on its own line

projects.title: LakeShark FT-891 app
projects.tagline: A built-in app for the LakeShark handheld-SDR firmware that turns an ESP32-P4 board into a pocket FT-891 remote.
projects.body:
LakeShark is community firmware for ESP32-P4 handhelds. This app adds a USB-host driver for the
radio's CAT port and sound card, a rigctld-compatible server, and big-button RIG/LINK screens, and it
feeds the radio's audio into LakeShark's FT8 decoder. It replaced an earlier standalone-firmware
attempt and is still in progress. Along the way: an upstream fix so the RTL-SDR Blog V4's USB strings
are read in full, which unlocks its HF mode.

projects.title: Orbic SDR server
projects.tagline: A rooted LTE hotspot turned into a Wi-Fi RTL-SDR server, with no reflash.
projects.body:
The hotspot (Qualcomm MDM9607) ships with its USB port locked to peripheral mode and no host
controller in the kernel. Three out-of-tree kernel modules, built against the matching vendor kernel,
add one at runtime and push the OTG state machine into host mode. With a powered hub, each RTL-SDR
dongle gets its own IP serving rtl_tcp, survives reboots, and appears on a custom SDR-themed status
screen. It fed an rtl_433 sensor logger (since retired) and the Cascata iOS app.

projects.title: Cascata
projects.tagline: An iOS receiver for rtl_tcp SDR servers, with a Metal waterfall.
projects.body:
SwiftUI with a GPU waterfall and spectrum and seven full-screen visualisers. WFM (stereo and RDS),
NFM, AM and SSB demodulation runs on Accelerate, with noise reduction, CTCSS/DCS tone squelch, a
scanner over bookmark groups, squelch-triggered recording, two VFOs inside one passband and CHIRP
CSV import. App Store preparation is paused.

projects.title: FT8 receive station & live map
projects.tagline: A receive-only FT8 station that hopped bands around the clock and plotted every decode on a live map.
projects.body:
An HF loop and an RTL-SDR fed SDR++ and WSJT-X. A band-hopper followed a day/night plan on FT8
period boundaries, and a watchdog relaunched the chain when the dongle disappeared. A small
stdlib-only Python app turned WSJT-X's UDP feed into a Leaflet map with great-circle paths, licence
lookups and server-sent events, and spots went to PSK Reporter. Paused in November 2026.

projects.title: Handheld radio programming
projects.tagline: A scripted channel plan and a native-Linux firmware flash for a BTECH BF-F8HP PRO.
projects.body:
Rather than typing hundreds of channels into CHIRP, scripts regenerate them from sources (repeater
lists, FAA airband frequencies, NOAA weather, railroad channels) into fixed 100-channel zones, then
upload the image and verify it against a readback. The firmware was updated from Linux with the
open-source FlintWave KDH flasher (the vendor's updater is Windows-only), and every channel survived
byte for byte.

projects.title: SDR++ noise reduction
projects.tagline: Switchable noise reduction for SDR++ audio through PipeWire filter chains.
projects.body:
The routing changes with the mode: RNNoise for voice, a spectral denoiser for AM, and nothing for CW,
because RNNoise erases it. It follows whichever demodulator you pick in SDR++ within a few seconds,
and one key on the desk deck toggles it.

projects.title: NanoVNA toolkit
projects.tagline: Command-line tools for a NanoVNA-F V2, covering guided calibration, averaged SWR reports and overlay plots.
projects.body:
It measures SWR and impedance across the HF bands or at spot frequencies, runs software-corrected
high-resolution sweeps above 7.6 MHz, captures the LCD, and overlays runs for before-and-after
antenna comparisons.

images.caption: SWR baseline for an end-fed half-wave, with per-band zooms

projects.title: Network SDR server
projects.tagline: Four RTL-SDR dongles on a Jetson, each shared over the LAN with SpyServer.
projects.body:
It ran one SpyServer instance per dongle, so SDR++ and SDR# clients anywhere in the house could share
them. One lesson worth keeping: for RTL-SDR, SpyServer's `device_serial` is a USB index, not a serial
number. It was retired when the Jetson died.

projects.title: GMRS repeater monitor
projects.tagline: Recorded, transcribed and summarised traffic on a local GMRS repeater.
projects.body:
It cut each transmission, transcribed it with Whisper, summarised it with a local model, and matched
spoken callsigns against FCC licence records, with a web UI and an MCP server. Its OAuth-gated MCP
became the template for later connectors. It was retired with the SDR server that fed it.

projects.title: Spectrum sweeper station
projects.tagline: Three receivers that wandered slices of spectrum, detecting, labelling and recording what they found.
projects.body:
Signals were matched against a band plan and captured as audio and IQ, and each sweeper stepped aside
whenever a person connected to its dongle. It needed a from-scratch Python SpyServer client that can
retune, which SoapySpyServer can't. It was retired with the SDR server.

projects.title: Morse Beacon for Flipper Zero
projects.tagline: A Flipper Zero app that keys Morse station IDs and text beacons out of the Sub-GHz radio.
projects.body:
It sends CW and MCW (by toggling FSK). Text can be typed on the Flipper, sent from a phone over BLE
serial, or fed in on the UART pins. Transmit is region-gated, with safe fallbacks when a saved
frequency isn't allowed. It has been verified on air and submitted to the official Flipper apps catalog.

images.caption: Beacon mode, listening between timed IDs

projects.title: Flipper repeater controller
projects.tagline: A repeater controller for the Flipper Zero, with COR in, PTT out, a courtesy tone, a timeout timer and a CW ID.
projects.body:
Two real radios do the RF, and the Flipper decides when to key. The README explains why the Flipper
can't be the repeater itself: it has one synthesiser and runs half duplex.

projects.title: Kid-friendly mesh messenger watch
projects.tagline: Custom Meshtastic firmware that turns a LilyGO T-Watch S3 into a child's LoRa messenger.
projects.body:
It replaces the stock screen with a colourful UI: a big-key keyboard, incoming messages read aloud, a
"secret knock", and a Fun tab with a stopwatch, doodle pad, a virtual pet fed by family messages, an
8-ball, themes and an alarm. The watch has no GPS, so a "Who's near me?" card reports the nearest heard
node instead. A later release fixed about five minutes a day of clock drift by re-anchoring to the
crystal RTC.

projects.title: Meshtastic for Android Automotive
projects.tagline: A fork of the Meshtastic Android app that runs on a car's built-in Android Automotive OS.
projects.body:
It uses the F-Droid flavour (osmdroid maps need no API key) plus the automotive manifest features, and
is built as an app bundle for Google Play's Automotive track so it can be tested in the car.

projects.title: Vellum for the T-Deck Pro MAX
projects.tagline: A paper-smartphone shell for an e-paper LoRa handheld that keeps the Meshtastic stack and replaces its UI.
projects.body:
Vellum swaps Meshtastic's on-device UI for a minimal smartphone-style shell on the LilyGO T-Deck Pro
MAX's e-paper screen. The design calls for messages, a map, an .epub reader, music and an LTE console,
built in phases. The project keeps a chapter-by-chapter journal of bring-up, power, the modem and
recovery.

projects.title: Desk control surface
projects.tagline: A Bluetooth knob and an open-source stream-deck setup wired into the radio, the GPUs and the lights.
projects.body:
The knob cycles through modes (volume, scroll, zoom, scrub, undo, lights and radio), with an Input
Remapper preset per mode switched over D-Bus. In radio mode the shack console reads the knob directly
to tune the FT-891. Deck keys show GPU stats, toggle SDR noise reduction and drive the RGB lighting.

projects.title: Headless 3D printing CLI
projects.tagline: Scripts that drive a Bambu Lab P1S without the slicer GUI.
projects.body:
The scripts flatten Bambu Studio's inherited profiles so the command-line slicer can use them, score
an STL's possible orientations, render previews, read printer status over MQTT and grab camera frames.
The printer still refuses a remote print-start, so starting a print stays a button press.

projects.title: Family assistant over iMessage
projects.tagline: A family assistant you text over iMessage, running on a local LLM with household tools.
projects.body:
One n8n agent serves every front end: iMessage, Discord and the TV's chat character. Its tools cover
the family calendar, the offline library, the bird detector, the solar inverter, the TV and local web
search, plus memory of past conversations and "errands" that keep relayed messages in context. It
sends a few short scheduled texts each day. iMessage goes through a bridge in a macOS VM, so the
assistant has its own Apple ID, and the model runs at home.

projects.title: Local LLM server
projects.tagline: One local model on two consumer GPUs, shared by every AI feature on this page.
projects.body:
llama.cpp's llama-server runs a 27B Qwen 3.8 finetune (Q4_K_M) with a multi-token-prediction draft
head and vision, split across an RTX 5070 Ti and an RTX 4070 on OCuLink. Measured along the way:
without GPU peer-to-peer, tensor parallel gains 35–40% decode but loses 30–50% prefill, so it wins for
chat and agent loops. A finite reasoning budget ended runaway thinking, and moving from Q5 to Q4
stopped a silent CPU spill-over, taking decode from about 35 to 42–55 tokens/s. Small shims let Claude
Code and a qFlipper fork talk to it.

projects.title: Offline reference library
projects.tagline: 381 GiB of offline reference (Wikipedia, medical, repair and preparedness libraries) that the assistant can search.
projects.body:
Thirty-two Kiwix ZIM books are served on the home network, so they still work when the internet
doesn't. About 21,600 PDFs inside the ZIMs were OCR'd, using the text layer or Apple's Vision OCR for
scans, so search hits come back with page numbers. An MCP server lets the assistant search and quote
the library. A daily "Library Find" shares one passage; the model only picks sentence numbers, so it
can't misquote.

projects.title: karaoke-tts
projects.tagline: A local MCP server that reads text aloud in a karaoke-style player with word-by-word highlighting.
projects.body:
Kokoro synthesises the audio in small chunks that stream to the browser over WebSocket, so playback
starts within seconds. faster-whisper then refines each chunk's word timings, and every reading is
saved as an OGG and HTML pair.

projects.title: OpenClaw assistant (v1)
projects.tagline: The family assistant's first version, an OpenClaw gateway on a local model.
projects.body:
It ran the assistant through OpenClaw with a local Gemma 4 31B. A smaller mixture-of-experts model
was faster but couldn't reason well enough for it. It was replaced by the n8n-based assistant in November 2026.

projects.title: Image upscaler
projects.tagline: A small CLI that upscales and refines an image through Google's Gemini image model.
projects.body:
It wraps the Gemini image API with a strict system prompt that always returns an image, never a chat
reply, and asks it to sharpen details while keeping any text intact, at a chosen output resolution.

projects.title: Living-room TV launcher
projects.tagline: A debloated Google TV with a custom pixel-art home screen and a resident cartoon cat who reviews whatever's on.
projects.body:
The stock launcher is gone. Home shows pixel-art holiday scenes and a voxel cat with moods and
costumes. A vision model watches periodic screenshots and posters to write the cat's reactions. It also
pops up behind-the-scenes facts that are cold-checked against their sources, where every number must
appear in the source. Weather and alerts, timers and reminders round out Home. An MCP server drives
the TV over ADB, so Claude and the family assistant can control it.

projects.title: Talk to the TV cat
projects.tagline: Press OK and talk to the TV's cartoon cat, who answers in character with kid-safe tools.
projects.body:
The app records the TV's built-in far-field mic. Parakeet transcribes it in about 60 ms on CPU (it
beat Moonshine and Whisper on a bench of kid-style questions), and the family assistant answers with
a kid-safe tool set and the cat's persona, thinking disabled for speed. The reply streams back with a
meow "typing blip" and the cat's mood on its face.

projects.title: Voxel cat
projects.tagline: A three.js renderer that turns the TV cat's pixel sprite into a 3D character, in four styles and eleven moods.
projects.body:
Build scripts paste the launcher's sprite data into one HTML file, which renders it as voxels, low-res
pixel 3D, vinyl toy or low-poly, with hand-drawn faces for each mood. The voxel style now runs live on
the TV's home screen.

images.caption: The voxel style, as it runs on the TV's home screen

projects.title: YouTube screen-time guard
projects.tagline: A daily limit and a bedtime for YouTube on the family TV, enforced inside the custom launcher.
projects.body:
Nothing built in fit, so the launcher reads app-usage events every few seconds and locks YouTube once the
day's allowance is spent or it's bedtime. Other apps stay free. A grown-up can unlock it with a text to
the family assistant. The rules are pure functions with their own tests.

projects.title: Solar & battery inverter dashboard
projects.tagline: Monitoring and guarded controls for a hybrid solar/battery inverter over Modbus and MQTT.
projects.body:
It keeps 30 days of readings and serves a mobile-first dashboard with its own SVG charts and a
power-flow view. A Controls tab writes only an allowlist of settings: output and charge priority,
charge and discharge windows, and the inverter clock. Every write is read back and audited, and
battery settings are never writable. MCP tools are read-only or preview-first.

projects.title: Time-of-use demand modeling
projects.tagline: Simulates a utility's demand-charge tariff from 15-minute data and acts to keep the monthly peak down.
projects.body:
It pulls per-circuit and meter data, reproduces the time-of-use bill to within 2% of real bills, and
attributes the demand charge to individual circuits so what-if questions get real answers. During peak
hours it alerts on spikes and pre-heats or pre-cools through the thermostats beforehand, skipping mild
days.

projects.title: Backyard bird detector
projects.tagline: Self-hosted bird ID from outdoor camera microphones, using Cornell's Merlin sound models.
projects.body:
RTSP audio is cut into roughly three-second windows and run through the Merlin TFLite models, with a
geographic prior and a bird/not-bird gate. Detections land in SQLite behind a journal and grid
dashboard, a morning report and an MCP server. Merlin's model bundle is Cornell's and isn't in the repo.

projects.title: Web NVR
projects.tagline: A browser-based network video recorder that finds RTSP cameras on its own.
projects.body:
It scans the network for RTSP cameras and streams them live as low-latency HLS, with WebSocket status
updates, per-camera start and stop, and SQLite-backed configuration.

projects.title: Self-documenting home lab
projects.tagline: A private wiki that rebuilds itself every night from what's actually running, plus cross-host backups.
projects.body:
Collectors inventory the containers, services, scheduled jobs and repos on each machine. A generator
joins those facts with a hand-curated catalog and rebuilds a private MkDocs wiki that flags drift and
unpushed work. Restic backs each machine up to the other and to object storage.

projects.title: Linkover
projects.tagline: Send a link from your iPhone's share sheet and it opens on your Linux or Mac desktop.
projects.body:
A tray or menu-bar client for GNOME and macOS that listens on Pushover's WebSocket API, so there's no
polling and no always-on server. Incoming links open in the browser, and the last ten are one click
away.

projects.title: Music library fixer
projects.tagline: Cleans up a messy music library with acoustic fingerprints and MusicBrainz.
projects.body:
It identifies tracks by sound with Chromaprint and AcoustID, pulls the metadata from MusicBrainz,
handles compilations properly, and reorganises files into Artist/Album (Year)/Track for Plex. File moves
are atomic and verified, with rollback.

projects.title: This project index
projects.tagline: The page you're reading, rebuilt daily from the projects on my machines.
projects.body:
A daily job reads activity from local git repos and GitHub, refreshes screenshots of safe views, and
renders this static page. A privacy scan checks the whole output against a deny-list (names, places,
hostnames, addresses, callsigns, tokens) before anything is pushed. New private projects wait for review,
and changed images wait for approval.

use_cases.title: The "boot loop" that was my own serial console
use_cases.problem: A freshly flashed ESP32-P4 handheld seemed to reboot itself again and again, with a 30-second splash each time.
use_cases.approach:
The reboots lined up exactly with each new serial connection, and the firmware's crash record showed only external
resets. The board wires the USB-serial chip's DTR/RTS lines straight to the chip's EN pin, so Linux toggling them on
every port open reset the board. A tiny helper now holds the port open in a state Linux leaves alone, run as a
systemd service tied to that USB device.
use_cases.outcome: Connecting no longer resets the board. It still resets once on plug-in and when flashing, as it should.
use_cases.lesson: If a board "boot-loops" only while you're watching it, suspect your own tooling first.

use_cases.title: Two different reasons for "CARRIER: WAITING"
use_cases.problem: The FM screen of a handheld SDR firmware sat on "waiting for carrier" with no audio, on two separate occasions.
use_cases.approach:
The first time, reading the firmware source showed the screen was locked to a frequency below the onboard LR2021's
floor, a job the firmware hands to an external RTL-SDR that wasn't plugged in. The second time, the console showed no
dongle registered at all. A reboot and USB root-port resets didn't help, and the schematic showed the USB-A power
switch's enable pin tied to 5 V, so no software can cut the dongle's power.
use_cases.outcome: Retuning fixed the first case. The second needed a physical unplug and replug, after which HF came straight back.
use_cases.lesson: A bus-powered dongle that hangs stays hung until VBUS drops, and a reboot doesn't drop it.

use_cases.title: An invisible mouse pointer that was really a VRAM shortage
use_cases.problem: The mouse pointer vanished on the Linux desktop, but hovering and clicking still worked.
use_cases.approach:
The GNOME log lines looked like a multi-GPU modifier bug, but a kernel NVKMS error showed the display GPU couldn't
allocate memory for the cursor sprite. The local LLM server had sized itself to leave only 512 MiB free, and the
desktop ate that. Fixing the per-GPU margin was complicated by llama.cpp numbering the GPUs in the reverse of
nvidia-smi's order.
use_cases.outcome: A bigger per-device margin on the display GPU fixed it for good. The pointer only comes back after a fresh login.
use_cases.lesson: Pointer position needs no GPU memory and the sprite does, which is why input keeps working. Mutter falls back to a software cursor for the rest of the session.

use_cases.title: Most "freezes" were failed resumes from sleep
use_cases.problem: A workstation seemed to freeze at random every few days and needed a hard reset.
use_cases.approach:
An audit of all 36 retained boots found 14 ending with "PM: suspend entry" as the last log line, so the desktop was
suspending itself after 15 idle minutes (SSH doesn't count as activity) and failing to resume. A remote kernel log
stream (netconsole) caught the remaining hangs from another machine.
use_cases.outcome: Masking the sleep targets ended the suspend failures. A smaller set of real hangs under dual-GPU load is still being chased.
use_cases.lesson: Before debugging a "hang", check whether the machine simply went to sleep.

use_cases.title: A hard freeze, and the crash log that had quietly stopped working
use_cases.problem: The workstation hard-froze twice in half an hour. The journal stopped mid-line with no kernel, GPU or PCIe error.
use_cases.approach:
A service that logged every 7.5 seconds pinned the freeze to the second, below where the kernel's lockup watchdog
could see it. Both freezes came while the LLM was busy across both GPUs, one of them on an OCuLink link. The remote
netconsole log that should have caught it had stopped days earlier, because the receiving machine's MAC address
changed after a network-card swap.
use_cases.outcome: No root cause yet, though the evidence points at the PCIe link under dual-GPU load. Netconsole works again and now checks the MAC.
use_cases.lesson: Netconsole fails silently when the receiver's MAC changes, so test your crash logging before you need it.

use_cases.title: Black screen after the monitor sleeps
use_cases.problem: After the monitor went to sleep, the screen often never came back, and sometimes the only fix was a reboot.
use_cases.approach:
The kernel log showed "HDMI FRL link training failed". The monitor's 240 Hz mode needs HDMI 2.1's FRL signalling,
and the NVIDIA driver often fails to retrain it after a display power event. A rescue script, runnable over SSH, drops
to a 60 Hz mode that always trains and then retries the full mode.
use_cases.outcome: The real fix is to use DisplayPort for this pairing. The script covers the times the cabling can't change.

use_cases.title: "Downloads keep failing": four causes, three of them local
use_cases.problem: Browser downloads failed and pages stalled on and off for months, on both wired and Wi-Fi.
use_cases.approach:
`ethtool` showed the link partner had withdrawn gigabit from its advertisement, so a failing cable kept flapping the
link and downshifting it to 100 Mb. A Flatpak sync service in a restart loop was quietly using about 30 Mbps. The
router advertised IPv6 that black-holed some sites. The real path MTU was 1420, not 1500.
use_cases.outcome: A new cable took throughput from about 9 to 22 MB/s with peaks near 90. Masking the runaway service and turning IPv6 off on that profile cleared the stalls.
use_cases.lesson: Check the negotiated link speed first. An intermittent fault often has more than one cause.

use_cases.title: A permission prompt nobody could click froze a headless Mac
use_cases.problem: Two services on a headless Mac mini, a bird detector and an inverter monitor, hung with no error. Even their SQLite opens never returned.
use_cases.approach:
Sampling a hung process showed it stuck in the kernel's `open()`. Sampling the per-user privacy daemon (tccd) showed
its threads piled up behind a consent prompt nobody could answer. The root cause: macOS ties these grants to a
binary's path, and each Homebrew upgrade of node or python changes that path.
use_cases.outcome: Force-killing tccd let both services recover, and moving their data out of the protected Documents folder keeps it from recurring.
use_cases.lesson: On a headless Mac, keep service data out of TCC-protected folders.

use_cases.title: Two apps quietly rendering on the CPU
use_cases.problem: SDR++ used about 830% CPU drawing a waterfall, and a 3D slicer felt sluggish, on a machine with two NVIDIA GPUs.
use_cases.approach:
SDR++ ran in a distrobox created without NVIDIA support, so OpenGL fell back to llvmpipe. Rather than rebuild the
container, the host's NVIDIA libraries were symlinked in and registered with glvnd. The slicer had a months-old
Flatpak override forcing software GL.
use_cases.outcome: SDR++ dropped to 1–2% CPU on the GPU. Resetting the override restored hardware rendering in the slicer.
use_cases.lesson: Check `glxinfo -B`. Old workarounds outlive the bugs they fixed.

use_cases.title: Every GNOME extension silently switched off
use_cases.problem: A keep-awake extension wasn't running, and it turned out every GNOME extension had been off for days.
use_cases.approach:
Three GNOME Shell crashes, the last within two seconds of startup, had tripped a safety switch that disables user
extensions, on the theory that an extension caused the crash. The actual crash was in the shell's sound-device code.
The first check said everything was fine because the terminal's `gsettings` was Homebrew's build, which can't see the
real settings.
use_cases.outcome: Flipping the setting back restored all 15 extensions without a restart.
use_cases.lesson: On a system with Homebrew, call /usr/bin/gsettings. Brew's build returns defaults and silently drops writes.

use_cases.title: A global setting flipped which GPU an app used
use_cases.problem: An image-generation launcher that pinned work with CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1,0 started computing on the wrong card.
use_cases.approach:
Testing all four combinations of CUDA_DEVICE_ORDER and CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES in PyTorch showed that a system-wide
PCI_BUS_ID setting, added two weeks earlier for another app, had inverted the old workaround.
use_cases.outcome: The launcher now sets both variables explicitly, so the bigger card is always the compute device.
use_cases.lesson: A workaround written for one enumeration order breaks the moment something else changes the order.

use_cases.title: An audio interface that fell off USB on its own
use_cases.problem: A USB audio interface kept going "offline", sometimes at 4 a.m. with nothing playing.
use_cases.approach:
A small monitor service polled every five seconds and saved diagnostics for each event. The signature was always a
clean USB disconnect and a re-enumeration a second later, with no host-side errors, on a direct root-hub port, and in
escalating bursts. That pointed at the device's power path, not drivers or firmware.
use_cases.outcome: Firmware reflashing and custom drivers were ruled out. A staged A/B plan swaps the power adapter, the cable, and then the port.
use_cases.lesson: Log faults automatically before you theorise. Manual power cycles look exactly like faults in the logs.

use_cases.title: Tracing radio noise to a monitor's power supply
use_cases.problem: The noise floor on several receivers jumped up to 20 dB in a single step, with a flat hash and no carrier.
use_cases.approach:
The hash pulsed at exactly 250 Hz with strong harmonics, which pointed to power electronics, not mains. Turning the
workstation off didn't clear it, and the solar inverter was ruled out by its logs. The sudden step turned out to be a
coax run falling behind an OLED monitor. Weeks later it came back on a long HF wire.
use_cases.outcome: Turning the monitor off dropped the floor by 8 dB immediately, and rerouting the coax fixed it.
use_cases.lesson: A real signal's modulation lives only in its own channel, while hash stamps the same envelope rate on every frequency. Compare envelope spectra across bands.

use_cases.title: SDR dongles dropping off USB, and the hub that caused it
use_cases.problem: On a four-dongle SDR server, dongles kept vanishing and the repeater monitor went silently deaf for 11 days.
use_cases.approach:
Each dropped dongle shifted the device indices, so SpyServer instances grabbed the wrong dongle or none at all. Per-port
power cycling with uhubctl made recovery possible remotely. A grabbed recording of pure FM hiss ruled out a decoding
bug.
use_cases.outcome: The USB sub-hub turned out to be the fault, not the dongles. Index-based device mapping is what made one drop cascade.
use_cases.lesson: When devices are addressed by index, one flaky device misroutes all the others. Pin devices by serial number wherever possible.

use_cases.title: SDR++ kept playing into the headphone jack
use_cases.problem: SDR++ audio landed on a USB card's headphone output while everything else went to its speakers.
use_cases.approach:
Probing the RtAudio library directly showed its PulseAudio backend sees one device name for a card that PipeWire
splits into three sinks. SDR++ couldn't address the speaker sink at all. Config edits and PipeWire routing rules
both lost to RtAudio's explicit choice.
use_cases.outcome: A launcher wrapper moves the stream to the right sink once SDR++ opens it.
use_cases.lesson: When an app can't name the device you want, move its stream after the fact.

use_cases.title: The CW "noise" that was really the AGC
use_cases.problem: Even with noise reduction on, a howl filled the gaps between Morse characters in SDR++.
use_cases.approach:
Recording and analysing the audio disproved the first theory, noise. The CW AGC was raising gain by up to 140 dB in
every pause. RNNoise, which the voice modes use, turned out to erase CW entirely, a repeater's Morse ID included.
use_cases.outcome: The noise reduction now routes by demodulator. The CW howl is a property of SDR++'s AGC, and is livable.
use_cases.lesson: Speech denoisers delete CW, RTTY and FT8, so route by mode.

use_cases.title: The radio console that started listening to the room
use_cases.problem: The browser "listen" feature on the radio console sounded like a room microphone, and the CW decoder printed false characters.
use_cases.approach:
When the radio's USB audio interface dropped off, PipeWire silently switched capture to the default input, which was a
webcam mic. Capture is now pinned to the interface by name and reconnects automatically. The false characters came
from input clipping and the decoder locking onto noise.
use_cases.outcome: Clipping went from 5.5% to zero, and false characters from about 245 a minute to none in a 60-second test. Probabilistic word-splitting raised whole-word accuracy from about 40% to 90%.
use_cases.lesson: After a USB drop, the sound server re-routes capture quietly, so pin it by device name.

use_cases.title: Building a transmit-capable radio console without ever transmitting
use_cases.problem: A web console for an HF radio had to handle real transmit paths for a brand-new operator, without ever keying the radio by accident.
use_cases.approach:
Receive-only is the default and is enforced in the CAT layer. A licence-privilege engine from FCC Part 97 decides
what's allowed where, and it and every transmit path were tested only against a simulated radio, in dozens of
safety cases. Polling the S-meter fast enough meant raising CAT from 4800 to 38400 baud.
use_cases.outcome: Receive, FT8 and CW decoding, band conditions and memory editing all work on the real radio, with no transmissions.
use_cases.lesson: One CAT command (AGC) flipped the radio from USB to LSB, which is firmware behaviour, not a bug in the app.

use_cases.title: "No FT8 signals" was really a stale clock
use_cases.problem: A handheld ESP32-P4 SDR decoded nothing on 40 m FT8.
use_cases.approach:
The firmware's built-in FT8, FT4 and WSPR self-tests all passed, so the decoder was fine. The board's real-time clock
was weeks off, and with no GPS or Wi-Fi nothing corrected it. A time-set command that landed late left it about
20 seconds slow.
use_cases.outcome: With the clock set, 20 m gave 42 decodes in two minutes, at SNRs from −1 to −18 dB.
use_cases.lesson: FT8 needs the clock within about a second. A bad clock looks exactly like a dead band.

use_cases.title: Measuring an antenna with unlabelled calibration parts
use_cases.problem: A new NanoVNA arrived with OPEN, SHORT and LOAD caps that weren't labelled, and the goal was SWR across four HF bands.
use_cases.approach:
Claude drove the VNA over its USB text shell and identified each cap from its readings; open and short, for example,
sit about 180° apart in phase. It calibrated 1–31 MHz, saved the calibration, and plotted SWR per band. The scripts
then became a small toolkit.
use_cases.outcome: 80 m and 10 m matched well (SWR 1.13 at 3.55 MHz), 40 m and 20 m sat around 2–3:1, and 20 m resonated about 300 kHz high.
use_cases.lesson: Placing a marker off the calibrated grid silently drops the VNA to factory calibration. SWR measured at the VNA end also looks better than it is because of cable loss.

use_cases.title: A repeatable noise-floor test for antenna changes
use_cases.problem: "Did moving the antenna help?" kept getting answered by impression.
use_cases.approach:
A sweep script drives a direct-sampling RTL-SDR over rtl_tcp across seven centre frequencies from 0.3 to 14.3 MHz.
The levels are uncalibrated, so a run is only compared against another run with the same dongle and settings.
use_cases.outcome: Before-and-after numbers for every change, and a saved baseline to compare against.
use_cases.lesson: Give the tuner a few seconds after each retune, or a settle bug produces confidently wrong numbers.

use_cases.title: Two mesh radios that may not have been on the same frequency
use_cases.problem: Messages on a private Meshtastic channel stopped arriving between two devices.
use_cases.approach:
Meshtastic derives the frequency slot from a hash of the channel name unless it's set explicitly, so the same channel
can sit on different frequencies across firmware setups. A third device listened receive-only on both candidate
frequencies, keeping to a standing no-transmit rule.
use_cases.outcome: Nothing was heard from the sender on either frequency. It turned out to be reporting zero airtime, and the likeliest culprit was a phone-to-node Bluetooth link that had gone stale. Reboots cleared it.
use_cases.lesson: Set the frequency slot explicitly, and a "connected" Bluetooth link can still be dropping messages.

use_cases.title: A brand-new Wi-Fi 7 card on an immutable Linux
use_cases.problem: The motherboard's MediaTek MT7927 Wi-Fi/Bluetooth had no kernel support yet, and Bluetooth sat in an endless probe loop.
use_cases.approach:
Wi-Fi uses an out-of-tree mt76 build loaded by a systemd unit, with its modules relabelled `modules_object_t` so
SELinux lets init load them. Bluetooth uses a checksum-verified firmware blob the kernel finds through
`firmware_class.path`, set by a tmpfiles rule.
use_cases.outcome: Both work, and both are written to retire themselves once the kernel and linux-firmware catch up.
use_cases.lesson: Kernel arguments staged on an atomic distro only finalise on a clean shutdown, and a hard lock throws them away.

use_cases.title: A flashing script that clobbered the OTA partition
use_cases.problem: Meshtastic nodes flashed with the bundled install script misbehaved on 16 MB boards.
use_cases.approach:
The script reads the correct filesystem offset from the release metadata, then flashes at a hard-coded address
anyway, which lands inside the OTA partition on 16 MB layouts. Flashing each image by hand with esptool, at the
offsets from the release's partition table, fixed it.
use_cases.outcome: Several nodes were flashed cleanly this way, including an 8 MB board that needs different offsets.
use_cases.lesson: Trust the release's partition table over the script that ships with it. Read config back after every write too, because writes over TCP can be silently lost.

use_cases.title: Writing a throwaway firmware just to format an SD card
use_cases.problem: A handheld's firmware could see its SD card but not read it, and it has no format command.
use_cases.approach:
The card turned out to be exFAT, which the firmware can't read. After confirming the bootloader doesn't check
signatures, Claude built a purpose-made formatter in an ESP-IDF container and flashed it into the app slot. It checked
the card, formatted it FAT32 and verified it with a test file, then the original firmware went back on.
use_cases.outcome: The 64 GB card mounted, and the device's settings were untouched.
use_cases.lesson: On small firmwares, "seen but unmountable" usually means exFAT.

use_cases.title: Turning a microcontroller into a USB card reader
use_cases.problem: The goal was to load an offline street map and 600 MB of music onto a handheld's SD card, but copying over the serial console would have taken hours.
use_cases.approach:
Temporary firmware turned the board into a high-speed USB mass-storage device. The map was cut from free
OpenStreetMap-based Protomaps data and converted to PMTiles, and the music was converted to plain 16-bit WAV, with
every file verified byte for byte.
use_cases.outcome: All the files copied in about 24 minutes and the map shows street-level detail. A bigger USB buffer didn't help, because the card's small-write speed (about 0.4 MB/s) was the real limit.
use_cases.lesson: If the device doesn't appear on the USB bus at all, check whether the cable is charge-only.

use_cases.title: A printed case built from the manufacturer's STLs, with a magnet inside
use_cases.problem: An e-paper LoRa handheld needed a removable case that cleared every port, with an embedded magnet ring.
use_cases.approach:
A parametric Python generator lofted case bodies from cross-sections of the manufacturer's published STLs. It was
checked for interference and floating islands, then iterated through snap case, clamshell, kickstand and embedded
magnet, with a slicer pause so the magnet is printed over.
use_cases.outcome: The snap case and clamshell printed and fit. The kickstand nubs were too small. The magnet print jammed because a project-level supports setting filled the cavity.
use_cases.lesson: Verify against the real slicer project, not a stock profile. A per-plate print-sequence override can grey out "Add pause".

use_cases.title: Remote printing, and the printer's cloud-mode lockout
use_cases.problem: The goal was to print an SDR dongle cage on a Bambu P1S straight from an STL, without touching the printer.
use_cases.approach:
Slicing the part on its edge with tree supports made the clip legs strong and cut the print from 2 h 25 m to 1 h 37 m.
A generic start G-code was swapped for the printer's real one, the file was uploaded, and progress was read over the
printer's local MQTT.
use_cases.outcome: The printer refused the remote print-start (error 0x05024007), so it was started from the app's file list and printed fine.
use_cases.lesson: In cloud mode, third-party start commands are blocked, so plan on pressing the button.

use_cases.title: RGB lighting that ignored its controller
use_cases.problem: OpenRGB couldn't control the motherboard lighting, didn't see the RAM at all, and later the fans wouldn't take colours.
use_cases.approach:
OpenRGB skips a board whose ARGB headers report zero LEDs, so the headers had to be set to 40. The RAM only appears
once a user is logged in, because a stale pre-login server held the bus. Fans on a 12 V header needed a small
direct-write module. A stdlib-only SDK client drives it all from deck keys.
use_cases.outcome: The deck controls power, colour, effects, brightness and fans, and the settings survive restarts.
use_cases.lesson: Read the state back from the hardware rather than trusting what the plugin thinks it set. The board also ignores "Direct" mode.

use_cases.title: Patching a startup crash in a prebuilt SDR++
use_cases.problem: SDR++ crashed with a divide-by-zero signal (SIGFPE) at startup.
use_cases.approach:
The waterfall code divides by its height before the height is set, a race at startup. The core library was rebuilt at
the exact commit the package came from, with guards in two functions (one also had a memmove size underflow).
use_cases.outcome: The crash is gone. Upgrading the package would overwrite the patched library, and the fix is recorded so it can be reapplied.
use_cases.lesson: Rebuild at the package's exact commit, so the patched library stays ABI-identical to the rest of the install.

use_cases.title: Testing a Flipper Zero app without touching the Flipper
use_cases.problem: Developing a Flipper Zero radio app meant pressing a lot of buttons to test each build.
use_cases.approach:
The serial CLI can drive a running app with `input send`. `loader info` reports whether it crashed and `free` checks
for leaks, so a script can smoke-test every build. That turned up traps: the CC1101's `begin()` returns false by
design, list-item pointers dangle after a rebuild, and asynchronous transmit drops the first and last level runs.
use_cases.outcome: The app was verified on air and submitted to the official app catalogue.

use_cases.title: Grafting a missing speculative-decoding head back into a model
use_cases.problem: Community "abliterated" exports of the local 27B model lacked the multi-token-prediction (MTP) head the server uses for speed.
use_cases.approach:
Comparing tensor counts (1,199 against 1,184) showed the 15 MTP tensors missing, because Transformers'
`save_pretrained` drops modules it doesn't know. Only those tensors were fetched from the stock shards, using HTTP
byte ranges, then grafted into the export's index. The result was converted to GGUF and quantised to Q4_K_M with the
reference model's per-tensor overrides and an importance matrix.
use_cases.outcome: A working build with draft-MTP engaged (about 39 tokens/s in a test), set up as a switchable alternative to the default model.
use_cases.lesson: Any tool that round-trips weights through Transformers can silently drop inference-only tensors.

use_cases.title: Pointing Claude Code at a local model
use_cases.problem: The goal was to run Claude Code against the home LLM server instead of a cloud API.
use_cases.approach:
llama.cpp already serves an Anthropic-compatible endpoint, so the base URL was enough. But Claude Code sends a
trailing system message after the user turn, which the model's chat template rejects, so a small shim folds it in.
Watching the process's sockets confirmed it never contacted anything off the machine. The same trick lets a qFlipper
fork that only speaks Ollama's API use the server.
use_cases.outcome: Plain prompts and full tool-call round trips work against the local model.
use_cases.lesson: Patch the message shape in a shim, not the shared model's template, which every other client depends on.

use_cases.title: The assistant that thought for six minutes
use_cases.problem: After a tool error, the family assistant's reasoning model thought for 342 seconds, hit the workflow timeout and left a typing indicator on.
use_cases.approach:
A finite reasoning budget on the server closes the thinking block so the model has to answer, and the token limit and
timeout were raised to match. Short replies turn thinking off per request.
use_cases.outcome: There have been no more runaway turns. A one-line reply went from 2.7 s to 1.3 s with thinking off.
use_cases.lesson: Reasoning models need a thinking budget in production. "Effort" alone doesn't bound it.

use_cases.title: Making an AI ask before it deletes, by enforcing it in code
use_cases.problem: An assistant with write access to the family calendar and lists removed items without asking, despite prompt rules telling it to confirm.
use_cases.approach:
A separate tool endpoint's first call only returns the question to ask. A change runs only after a later call with a
single-use confirmation code, which expires in five minutes, and only one change can be pending at a time. Deletes
must resolve to exactly one item and are verified afterwards.
use_cases.outcome: It was tested end to end. When the model fired the same "yes" about 30 times in a loop, only the first got through.
use_cases.lesson: Prompts ask, code enforces. Put destructive-action confirmation in the tool, not the system prompt.

use_cases.title: Picking speech-to-text for a TV that talks back
use_cases.problem: A voice chat on the family TV needed fast, accurate speech-to-text, with no GPU memory to spare.
use_cases.approach:
Six setups (Parakeet 0.6B, Moonshine, and Whisper small and large-v3-turbo) were benchmarked on a workstation CPU and
an Apple-silicon Mac, using clean and noisy clips of the kinds of things kids ask.
use_cases.outcome: Parakeet on the CPU won, at about 60 ms per utterance with near-zero errors and no GPU at all. Short names were the weak spot until the vocabulary was biased toward them.
use_cases.lesson: The fastest, most accurate option was the CPU one.

use_cases.title: Stopping trivia about the wrong thing
use_cases.problem: TV pop-up trivia showed facts about a garment for a YouTube channel whose name was one letter off from it. Wikipedia search had quietly "corrected" the unknown name.
use_cases.approach:
Every name word in the query must now appear in the matched article, and the fact-writer is told a name is never a
typo. Searches use the screenshot, title, channel and captions together, from narrow to broad.
use_cases.outcome: Wrong-subject facts are blocked in tests, and the improved search order is live.
use_cases.lesson: Checking that a fact matches its article isn't enough. Check that the article is about the original subject.

use_cases.title: "Get rid of the meow" added another meow
use_cases.problem: Asking the TV cat's music mode to remove a sound made it add another layer of that sound.
use_cases.approach:
Keyword rules always treated the word as a request to add. Removal intent ("remove", "no more", "mute", "take out")
now wins. Clear removals drop the matching layers without calling the LLM, and vague ones go to the LLM with a
delete-only instruction.
use_cases.outcome: Removal works for every instrument and sound, tested offline against the exact phrases that failed.
use_cases.lesson: Substring matching fires on "pulsing" and "rising" because they contain "sing". Intent keywords need word boundaries and ordering.

use_cases.title: When an LLM can't hum, look the tune up
use_cases.problem: The language model couldn't reliably recall famous melodies, so the TV cat's ocarina songs came out wrong.
use_cases.approach:
Songs come from a three-tier chain: a small public-domain songbook with exact notes, then free MIDI libraries (search,
download, and pull the lead track's top notes with mido, shifted into range and cached), and only then the model's
memory.
use_cases.outcome: Songbook and MIDI lookups play correctly. Some requests still find no MIDI file.
use_cases.lesson: Making the band louder buried the melody, so mix changes need a melody-priority check.

use_cases.title: Guarding an inverter's settings below the UI, not in it
use_cases.problem: A dashboard was getting controls for a solar inverter's charge windows and priorities, and the layer underneath could write far more than that.
use_cases.approach:
The Modbus-to-MQTT gateway accepted writes to every register, including battery type and voltages. Its register map was
replaced with one that's read-only except for an allowlist of 16 registers. The app adds value checks, a read-back
after every write, and an audit log, and its AI tools preview a change before applying it.
use_cases.outcome: The controls are live and tested on the real inverter, and the dangerous settings can no longer be written through the gateway.
use_cases.lesson: Hiding a setting in the UI protects nothing if a lower layer still accepts it.

use_cases.title: A phone dashboard that downloaded 13 MB to draw a chart
use_cases.problem: The inverter dashboard was slow on phones, pulling about 13 MB to show 30 days of history.
use_cases.approach:
The history query now buckets values on the server, using a covering index. The UI was rebuilt mobile-first, with a
power-flow diagram, touch charts, tap-to-see-history and a home-screen app manifest.
use_cases.outcome: Thirty days now loads 36 KB in about 180 ms.
use_cases.lesson: At the 30-day scale, the peak-window overlay turned into noisy stripes, so the overlay is dropped at that zoom.

use_cases.title: The TV that "died" was just very asleep
use_cases.problem: After a standby test, a debloated Google TV vanished from the network for almost seven hours.
use_cases.approach:
Android's system_server had crashed after a wake, and the chip fell into deep sleep with Wi-Fi off, so it ignored
network wake requests. It hadn't been bricked: it came back on its own.
use_cases.outcome: There's now a recovery procedure: press the remote's power button, then read the crash records.
use_cases.lesson: An unreachable embedded device isn't necessarily dead. Find out what power state it's in before assuming the worst.

use_cases.title: Recovering files from a crash-corrupted encrypted volume
use_cases.problem: A crash mid-write left an encrypted ext3 volume with missing files, zero-byte stubs and "Structure needs cleaning" errors.
use_cases.approach:
The decrypted device was copied to an image with dd and fsck was run on the copy. The journal had wrapped and undelete
tools found nothing, but about 1,000 orphan inodes still had intact block chains, and fsck reattached them with full
content. Signature carving found the rest, and partial MP4s were rebuilt from their raw H.264 units.
use_cases.outcome: About a thousand files came back with their full content. The live volume was repaired the same way only after the copy proved it worked.
use_cases.lesson: Run fsck on an image first. PhotoRec's auto-detected 64 KB block size truncates every file at 64 KB, so force 4096.

use_cases.title: Rescuing an overnight OCR job and the PDFs that hung it
use_cases.problem: An OCR job over about 21,600 PDFs in an offline library died after an OS update, and eleven PDFs hung or failed.
use_cases.approach:
An Xcode update had swapped the system Python for one that needs a licence accepted, so the standard-library-only
script moved to Homebrew Python. A Ghostscript rewrite fixed the books that hung. For truncated files, the page images
were pulled out with mutool, repacked and OCR'd.
use_cases.outcome: The job finished at about 815,000 pages, and 10 of the 11 bad books became searchable. The last one was all zeros at the source.
use_cases.lesson: The re-encode turned 4-hour hangs into 6-second jobs, so the hang was in the image decoder, not the book. Queue known-bad files last.

use_cases.title: Making 400 GB of offline books searchable by an assistant
use_cases.problem: An offline reference library, including scanned old books, needed to be searchable by the home assistant, on a nearly full machine.
use_cases.approach:
aria2 with nearby mirrors raised downloads from about 7 to 69 MB/s. For OCR, Apple's Vision framework running natively
beat Tesseract in Docker, at 0.44 against 1.6 seconds a page. OCR text lives in plain files with a rebuilt index,
rather than a SQLite database shared across the Docker VM boundary.
use_cases.outcome: The assistant answered a water-safety question by finding and quoting a scanned public-health PDF.
use_cases.lesson: Kiwix rejects searches that mix languages, so group the books by language.

use_cases.title: One-key bug reports from inside a game, screenshots included
use_cases.problem: GitHub's issues API can't take attachments, and bugs needed filing from inside the running game with a screenshot and a clip.
use_cases.approach:
A Vite dev-server plugin files the issue with the local gh CLI, so no token reaches the page. Media go into a secret
gist per issue, with ffmpeg turning the clip into a GIF because gists serve MP4 as a download. Each report includes a
"stand here again" link, console errors and GPU info, and forged-origin requests are refused.
use_cases.outcome: Merged. Test issues show the screenshot and the GIF inline.
use_cases.lesson: Save each report locally before uploading, so a failed upload loses nothing.

use_cases.title: An overnight AI developer that needs my approval to merge
use_cases.problem: Claude was to develop a side project unattended each night, but I can't approve pull requests opened under my own login.
use_cases.approach:
A systemd timer unloads the local LLM, runs fresh Claude sessions against the backlog, then brings the LLM back. A
GitHub App gives the bot its own identity, with an hourly token helper. A merge-rule engine, tested on 63 fixture
cases, handles drafts, hold labels, protected paths, CI and auto-merge timers, and a morning text sums up the night.
use_cases.outcome: Pull requests, CI, screenshot uploads, a mid-session token renewal and approval detection all worked end to end. A trial whole-codebase review found a real crash bug.
use_cases.lesson: A guard written too broadly, like blocking every PR that touches the agent's instructions file, quietly stalls everything. Check it against recent history.
